frameworks.name: Supply-First Sequencing in Capacity-Constrained Businesses
frameworks.definition: When demand exceeds delivery capacity, resolve supply constraints before increasing demand; prioritize hiring and training over sales expansion until fulfillment scales.

frameworks.name: Price-as-Talent-Signal Framework
frameworks.definition: Raising prices to the point of margin sufficiency enables recruiting and compensation upgrades to attract top talent, which compounds into a virtuous cycle of quality, reputation, and sustainable growth.

frameworks.name: Hat Maker Acquisition Model
frameworks.definition: Direct cold outreach to struggling trade artisans (hat makers, leather workers) offering significantly higher compensation in exchange for relocation and integration into a systemized operation at premium price points.

claims.text: A hat-making business at $800-1,200 per custom hat (virtual delivery, $2M revenue, 780k organic followers) that can double demand via paid ads but cannot scale fulfillment due to master hat maker scarcity is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodity or low-touch-delivery businesses where supply is easily fungible

claims.text: Hat making is not an inherent transferable skill; combining artistic vision with craft capability and customer-facing communication cannot be reliably trained from scratch.
claims.speaker: Anonymous hat business owner
bounded_by: May not apply to industries where component skills can be cleanly separated and trained independently

claims.text: When supply-constrained and generating strong margins (40-45% gross margin), raising prices and raising compensation proportionally is economically valid; a 30% talent cost increase funded by 30% price increase preserves margin while dramatically expanding the talent pool.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: demand remains stable through price increase
claims.mechanism: Price increase funds talent compensation increase, signaling better working conditions and enabling geographic/talent recruitment at higher quality thresholds without margin compression.
bounded_by: Does not apply to price-sensitive commodity markets where demand elasticity is high
Requires that the business has diagnosed supply (talent) as the true constraint, not demand

claims.text: Hat makers and artisans operating at break-even or negative margins in their own businesses present an underexploited recruitment pool; offering them double their current income plus the opportunity to execute craft in a systemized, well-capitalized environment is a strong value proposition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: target pool: existing trade practitioners in struggling solo practices or small shops
offer structure: salary bump + preserved craft focus
bounded_by: Does not apply when ego/autonomy needs dominate financial motivation
Some candidates will refuse due to unwillingness to work within systems

claims.text: Finding hat makers via cold-calling: search for hat-making business owners online, call them directly, and present relocation + employment opportunity as an upgrade to their struggling independent practice.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: niche trade skills exist in fragmented sole-proprietor market
cold outreach works best when offer is materially superior

claims.text: When a business is fully tapped out on delivery (current lead time 2-3 months, 40-45% margin, growing demand), pushing out delivery time further (to 6-8 months, industry standard) via demand expansion does not change customer acquisition because delivery time beyond 3-4 months psychologically represents indefinite wait.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: industry baseline 6-12 months for custom artisanal goods
claims.mechanism: At 3-4 month threshold, additional delay (to 6, 8, 12 months) does not further reduce demand because perception shifts from 'delayed' to 'indefinite'; therefore demand expansion that merely postpones delivery from 6 to 8 months captures no incremental value.

numbers.axis: delivery lead time vs demand elasticity

anchors.value: no differentiation from 6-12 month industry baseline

bounded_by: Does not apply to time-critical or perishable goods where weeks matter
Does not apply to commodities where shorter lead time is a competitive differentiator

claims.text: Supply-first strategy: resolve the hiring and training bottleneck (recruit 2-3 additional master hat makers) before pressing the 'demand button' to scale paid ads; hitting demand expansion before supply scales only delays fulfillment without increasing throughput.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: margin sufficient to fund talent upgrades

anchors.value: 2-3 additional hat makers needed to reach $5M

claims.text: Underpricing talent (paying below market, below what strong talent would accept) is a symptom of underpricing the product; a business offering high-margin goods ($800-1200 hats, 40%+ margin) that cannot recruit is not constrained by money—it is constrained by unwillingness to invest the margin into compensation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business is struggling to recruit despite adequate cash flow

examples.text: The Kentucky hat-maker business (selling custom $800-1,200 hats virtually via social media, 780k followers, $2M revenue) wants to hit $5M revenue. The owner noted they can 'slam the red button' to double paid ad spend and get 2x sales immediately, but fulfillment capacity is the constraint—it takes years to develop a master hat maker, and the skill combines artistic vision, craft execution, and customer-facing service. Current delivery window is 2-3 months, which is 2-4 months ahead of the 6-12 month industry standard for custom hats. When asked if expanding demand and pushing delivery to 6-8 months would help, Alex Hormozi replied no: beyond the 3-4 month inflection point, customers perceive all delays as equivalent (indefinite), so moving from 6 to 8 months changes nothing about customer behavior.

To recruit additional hat makers, the Kentucky business owner initially assumed recruiters wouldn't be able to source artisans. Hormozi suggested cold-calling existing hat-making business owners directly: 'I would just Google hat maker, and then I would call all the business owners.' The logic: existing hat makers are small-business owners, probably struggling financially, and likely don't have business acumen. If offered the chance to 'make the money you want to make and do the thing you want to do,' many will be attracted despite ego friction. For the Kentucky business at 2-3 additional hires needed to reach $5M from $2M, the cold-outreach supply unlock is realistic.

Alex Hormozi referenced his own team as a case study: when recruiting executives and high-level operators to Las Vegas, competitors' teams make $100-250k annually in some markets, plus perks. His team members make $300k on the low end, up to $750k+. The value prop: double the compensation, work with high-performing business owners in a systemized environment, trade the headache-to-payout ratio. 'Not all of them' will take the offer, but enough will that you can build an A-player team if you're willing to price for it. This illustrates that good talent is not scarce—it's just expensive.

practices.text: Resolve supply constraints before expanding demand; fix hiring, train talent, and scale fulfillment capacity before pressing the paid-ad acceleration button.
When supply-constrained, use margin to fund talent compensation increases rather than trying to recruit cheap; price the product to support top-tier salaries.

Source artisanal talent via cold outreach to existing trade practitioners; find them online, call directly, and offer compensation that exceeds their current independent earnings plus the appeal of a systems-backed operation.

Diagnose whether your constraint is truly supply (delivery, fulfillment, execution) or demand (traffic, awareness) before making growth investments; expanding demand into a supply constraint only delays delivery and sacrifices profit.
